images.text:
Kristi: Hi Adam! Have you been here long?
Adam: Not long. I got here, signed in and then went to a workshop on career guidance.
Kristi: Do you want to walk around for a bit? We can visit a few booths.
Adam: Sure, that's what I'm planning to do.
Kristi: So, how did you find that résumé writing workshop?
Adam: It was alright … boring. My friend told me he went to one and learned a lot of tips and tricks about how to write a résumé. I was hoping to learn a few more tricks, but I learned nothing!

Kristi: I know what you mean. There's another workshop later. I'm planning on going to that one.
Adam: I'm done with workshops today, maybe forever.
Kristi: Which booths have you visited?
Adam: Meh … I've only been to the art and culture section. I checked out a few public relations booths.
Kristi: Cool. Anything interesting?
Adam: There were a few copywriter positions and a market researcher position. That sounded interesting, I guess. I'm not sure I have the credentials for those positions.

Kristi: What does that position involve?
Adam: You have a lot of questions. According to the man at the booth, the type of work you do varies depending on your employer.
Kristi: I was talking to someone at the workshop. She told me about a multimedia specialist posting she came across. She said they were doing on the spot interviews.
Adam: On the spot interviews, you say? I'd like to do one of those while I'm here. I'm going to check that booth out.
Kristi: Well, good luck with it.

contents.value: Graham: I've been looking for new opportunities in marketing and advertising. I want to move into an art and culture work environment but I don't want to do market research anymore. Maybe Sam, who is a multimedia specialist for an art gallery, can give me some advice or point me in the right direction. Even though I don't have the experience or the credentials to know what I will be suited for, Sam does. She said there was a job in copywriting for the gallery if I wanted it, but I am not so sure about that.

Talking About Hopes And Expectations For The Future
Apart from using the Future tense to talk about the future, there are other verbs and patterns you can use to express hope and expectations for the future.

a. Hope + to + verb
“Hope” suggests that you want or expect something to be true in the future.
  • I was hoping to learn a few more tricks.
  • I hope to get an interview soon.

b. (be) + plan (-ing) + to + verb / (be) + plan (-ing) + on + -ing
“plan” indicates that you think carefully about actions that you need to take in order to achieve something.
  • I'm planning on going to that one too.
  • That's what I'm planning to do.
  • I'm planning to go for a walk soon.

c. be going to + verb
Use this structure to express the idea that you intend to do something in the future.
  • I'm going to check that booth out.
  • I'm going to look for a job here.

d. would like + to + verb
This structure can also be used to express the idea that you plan on doing something in the future.
  • I'd like to do of those while I'm here.
  • I'd like to start looking for a job while I'm here.
Reported Speech
You use reported speech when you are saying (reporting)  what other people said.
When you tell people what someone has said in the past, you generally make the verb tense 'more in the past'. You need to change the verb to the next past form.

For example:
Direct speech
  • I came across a multimedia specialist post.
Reported speech
  • She told me she had come across a multimedia specialist post.

When changing sentences from direct speech, check if you have to change the following:
  • pronouns (I said → He said)
  • Present tense verbs
  • Place and time expressions
  • Tenses (backshift → change to the past)
Some reporting verbs and expressions commonly used are: say, tell, and according to .
My friend told me he went to one and learned a lot of tips and tricks about how to write a résumé.
According to the man at the booth, the type of work you do varies depending on your employer.
She said they were doing on the spot interviews.
